content: Cutaneous drug eruptions are the most common type of adverse reactions to medications, with the majority being allergic in nature. These reactions can present in various forms, each with distinct clinical features: 1. Morbilliform Rash: This is the most frequently observed type of cutaneous drug eruption. It resembles a measles-like viral exanthem. The rash typically begins in dependent areas of the body and then spreads to become generalized. It usually appears 2 to 10 days after starting the offending drug but can also occur up to 14 days after the drug has been discontinued. 2. Urticaria: Urticaria, often associated with angioedema, is characterized by transient, raised, red, itchy, and well-defined lesions. These lesions resolve without leaving scars or hyperpigmentation. Urticaria can result from drug therapy. 3. Erythema Multiforme: Erythema multiforme minor is a cutaneous reaction that may initially resemble urticaria. The lesions are red, raised, and well-demarcated plaques that persist for several days to weeks. 4. Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN): TEN shares clinical features with Stevens-Johnson syndrome, including the types of causative drugs, fever, involvement of mucosal membranes, and full-thickness epidermal detachment. 5. DRESS Syndrome: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) is a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs. It presents with delayed-onset fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of internal organs such as the kidneys, liver, and/or heart. 6. Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis (LV): LV is a hypersensitivity reaction involving neutrophilic inflammation of the blood vessels in the skin. 7. Contact Dermatitis: Allergic contact dermatitis can occur with topical medications such as neomycin, benzocaine, and diphenhydramine. It presents as asymmetrically distributed, red, itchy papules and vesicles, characteristic of acute eczematous dermatitis. This is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells, also known as delayed-type hypersensitivity. 8. Fixed Drug Eruption: A fixed drug eruption is a less common type of drug-induced skin reaction. It manifests as a solitary, red, itchy macule that evolves into a raised plaque or blister. These plaques are typically 2 to 4 cm in diameter. Common causative agents include tetracycline, phenolphthalein (a laxative), and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. A skin biopsy can aid in diagnosis. 9. Photosensitive Drug Eruption: Photosensitive drug eruptions occur on sun-exposed skin and are classified as either phototoxic or photoallergic reactions. Phototoxic Reactions: These occur when drugs such as sulfonamides, tetracyclines, or psoralens absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation, releasing energy that damages epidermal cells. Clinically, this manifests as an exaggerated sunburn, but other morphologies, including bullous eruptions and hyperpigmentation, can also occur. Photoallergic Reactions: These occur when UV radiation causes a drug hapten to bind to native proteins in epidermal cells, forming a complete antigen that sensitizes nearby lymphocytes. This results in a pruritic, eczematous rash on sun-exposed areas.
